content: RoleCall RoleCall — config management & orchestration. A dual-runtime Ansible alternative: one executable that runs as a CLI (rolecall playbook run …) and as an orchestrator server (rolecall --serve). Status: Execution is live. playbook run applies state over SSH/local transports, facts gather collects targeted/cached facts per host, plugin list/register persist and auto-load user module plugins, --inventory consumes Ansible inventories (INI + all:-rooted YAML) directly by auto-detecting the format, and --tags/--skip-tags plus play-level handlers:/tags: cover Ansible-style selection and notifications. Transport + the executor are implemented, on Node.js ( =22.19, via npm) as well as Bun. Still scaffolded (do not treat as functional): scheduler / cron / webhooks / SPA UI route registry, the richer Plugin SDK authoring surface, the full Jinja {{ }} renderer (only structured references $var/$concat/$call/$if/$each/$template + typed when/loop exist), the Postgres backend (record-only), and RBAC / Vault / WinRM target capabilities. Requirements - npm install: Node.js = 22.19.0 (no Bun needed) - Binaries / source checkout: Bun = 1.4.2 Install Run Design & architecture Design context for contributors and agents lives in design/: goals, roadmap (implemented vs scaffolded), component architecture, and transport-layer design The published user guide/API reference is in docs/. Project layout See .omo/plans/rolecall.md for the full work plan. --- Installing RoleCall installs from the npm registry and runs on Node.js, or as a Bun-native addition to a project: The npm package ships a Node bundle (lib/cli.js) built by bun run build:js (node scripts/build-js.mjs); prepack runs that build automatically so the baked version matches the release. npx rolecall works the same way. For local development / contributing: Runtime split: none. The full feature surface — playbook runs, facts, inventory, vars, docs, plugins, the durable SQLite store, and everything that boots it (--serve, --trace, --profile, run replay) — works on both runtimes. See Node.js support below. Running While developing directly from source: After an npm/global install, the rolecall command is available on your PATH: rolecall --serve (start the orchestrator HTTP server) works on Node too — see Node.js support. Building native binaries (--compile) Produce standalone executables with no runtime dependency using Bun's bundler: Binaries are written to dist/bin/ - and named after the project (package.json → rolecall, e.g. dist/bin/rolecall-linux-x64-musl). The entry point compiled is scripts/cli-native-entry.mjs, a tiny dispatch wrapper that routes --version/-v before delegating everything else to the unchanged src/cli/index.ts main(). Smoke test (core acceptance). After building, the host binary is executed automatically and its version verified: Cross-compilation & multi-OS builds The builder maps each requested platform to Bun's cross-compile override (BUN TARGET OVERRIDE). Because true cross-compilation needs Bun to fetch the remote runtime for the target OS, this machine (a Linux x64 box) can only produce and execute the Linux host artifact . Non-host targets (windows- , darwin- , freebsd- ) are still emitted so their paths exist, but they are never executed here — the builder logs a clear generated, unexecuted on host line plus a note when a file came out of the wrong toolchain. To get genuine non-host binaries, either run the build on the matching OS or let GitHub Actions do it: Each matrix job compiles for its own host OS and runs the produced binary there. Set BIN BUN (or BIN BIN PATH) to point at a custom bun executable. On Windows, use --windows-hide-console (via the builder's banner flags if needed) so the compiled exe does not open a stray console prompt; see the service notes. Running RoleCall as a Windows service rolecall --serve is a long-lived Express process. On Windows it should be managed as a service by a dedicated supervisor (there is no built-in Windows service installer): Tool Register a service Notes --------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------- NSSM nssm install Rolecall "C:\path\to\rolecall-windows-x64.exe" --serve Most popular; GUI + CLI, handles restarts/logging. WinSW Ship a rolecall.xml manifest + the WinSW binary, then winsw install rolecall.xml XML config; CI-friendly. Use the bundled .exe as the executable path. Shawl shawl add --name Rolecall -- cmd.exe /c "C:\path\to\rolecall-windows-x64.exe --serve" Small .NET tool; easy service lifecycle. Whichever you choose, pin the executable path to the correct published binary (dist/bin/rolecall-windows-x64) and consider --windows-hide-console semantics so no interactive terminal window appears. For non-Windows hosts, prefer systemd (unit ExecStart=/opt/rolecall/dist/bin/rolecall-linux-x64-musl --serve). Node.js support RoleCall ships two distribution channels from one codebase. The npm channel is Node.js : npm i -g rolecall (or npx rolecall) works on a machine with Node \= 22.19.0 and no Bun installed. The published bin is lib/cli.js, a bun build --target=node --packages=external bundle produced by bun run build:js (node scripts/build-js.mjs, run automatically by prepack). Bun remains the batteries-included channel : compiled binaries (npm run build-bin, untouched) and source-checkout dev (bun bin/rolecall.js, bun run dev). What works on Node (npm install): the full feature surface. - --help / --version, inventory show/list (native + Ansible formats) - playbook run over SSH (ssh2) and local transports - facts gather, vars list/trace, docs search/docs modules - plugin list/register, agent manifest - the sql builtin + idempotency cache via the SQLite PAL (node:sqlite; prints a one-time ExperimentalWarning to stderr on first use — expected) - the durable SQLite store, and therefore --serve, --trace, --profile, and run replay (ADR 0019: the store opens a runtime-selected synchronous sqlite handle through the PAL — bun:sqlite under Bun, node:sqlite under Node — with the same schema, pragmas, and BEGIN IMMEDIATE read-modify-write fencing) Why Bun still matters: - Binaries are Bun artifacts. Native binaries built with bun compile embed the Bun runtime. They run standalone regardless of what interpreter is on PATH, but they are Bun executables, not Node-compatible ones. Node users install via npm. - Dev ergonomics. Source-checkout dev (bun bin/rolecall.js, bun run dev) and the bun:test runner stay Bun-native. - Faster cold starts. Bun's startup cost is lower, which shows up in short-lived CLI invocations. Notes worth stating plainly: - The Node PAL implementations in src/pal/ .node.ts are real (node:sqlite, node:crypto, node:dns/promises, node:child process, node:fs/promises, node:http, process.stderr). The SSH PAL surface stays a stub on Node; product SSH goes through ssh2 directly and works on Node either way. - You can force detection explicitly with the ROLECALL RUNTIME environment variable during tests / debugging: ROLECALL RUNTIME=node ... or ROLECALL RUNTIME=bun .... The value is read at call time by detectRuntime() in src/util/runtime.ts. Testing The assertion suite imports bun:test, which is Bun-native and unavailable under plain Node without an extra transpiling loader we deliberately do not vendor. To still exercise the Node runtime through its own harness , CI runs a small node --test probe against the pure-JS runtime-detection module (src/util/runtime.ts), verifying ROLECALL RUNTIME overrides work on both runtimes. See .github/workflows/ci.yml. Security & packaging notes These inherited constraints affect how dependencies are installed and packaged: - ssh2 is installed with --omit=optional to avoid pulling native cpu-features / node-libssh2 bindings. See the ssh2 CVE surface in .omo/notepads/rolecall/issues.md. - undici is pinned = 8.5.0 (devDependency) to avoid keep-alive connection-pool poisoning (CVE-2026-6733). Product code does not import it (comment-only reference), so it does not constrain the Node engines floor. - Bun workers : only offload CPU-bound work via bun.workers (workers: N); worker threads support is partial — don't assume full Node worker parity. - These optional/native-dep semantics are preserved in build docs above; the compiled bundle embeds RoleCall's direct dependencies while respecting that some packages are intentionally optional at install time.
